theme: Create in me a clean heart, David’s penitential psalm
readingInstruction: Read Psalm 51. You read this psalm earlier in Unit 6. Today read it in its original setting, as David’s prayer right after Nathan confronted him. Read it slowly, as his own words.
settingTheScene: The title says, “A Psalm of David, when Nathan the prophet went to him, after he had gone in to Bathsheba.” You met this psalm in Unit 6 as a general prayer of repentance. Having now read 2 Samuel 11 and 12, you can hear it as a particular man’s prayer after a particular fall. Notice how little he says about the circumstances, and how much he says about God and his own heart.
observation: “Have mercy on me, O God, according to your steadfast love; according to your abundant mercy blot out my transgressions” (v. 1).
“Wash me thoroughly from my iniquity, and cleanse me from my sin!” (v. 2).
“Against you, you only, have I sinned and done what is evil in your sight” (v. 4).
“Behold, I was brought forth in iniquity, and in sin did my mother conceive me” (v. 5).
“Purge me with hyssop, and I shall be clean; wash me, and I shall be whiter than snow” (v. 7).
“Create in me a clean heart, O God, and renew a right spirit within me” (v. 10).
“Cast me not away from your presence, and take not your Holy Spirit from me” (v. 11).
“The sacrifices of God are a broken spirit; a broken and contrite heart, O God, you will not despise” (v. 17).
interpretation:
David begins with God’s character, not his own record. “According to your steadfast love… according to your abundant mercy.” He has no defense and no excuse, so he asks for mercy. Three words for sin appear again, as in Psalm 32: transgression, iniquity, and sin. And three requests: blot out, wash, cleanse. He knows the problem is deep.

Verse 4 is surprising. “Against you, you only, have I sinned.” David had sinned against Bathsheba and Uriah and the nation. Yet he says that the offense is against God. This does not deny the harm to others, but recognizes that every sin is first of all a rebellion against the Creator, whose law has been broken. When we see sin at that level, we understand why it requires forgiveness, not just repair.

Verse 5 is not an excuse but a confession of depth. David realizes that his sin did not come out of nowhere. It flows from a nature that has been bent since birth. The problem is not only what he did, but what he is. He needs more than a new start. He needs a new heart, and so he prays, “Create in me a clean heart.” The verb “create” is the one used in Genesis 1. Only God can make a new heart from nothing.

He also asks, “Take not your Holy Spirit from me.” He had seen what happened to Saul. His fear is of losing God’s presence, not of losing the throne. Then he asks for the joy of salvation and for a willing spirit.

The psalm ends with the great principle: “The sacrifices of God are a broken spirit.” God does not need religious performance as a substitute for repentance. A broken and contrite heart he will not despise. He receives the one who comes with nothing.
connection: Jesus is the answer to David’s prayer. By his blood we are washed (1 John 1:7; Revelation 1:5), and in him we are a new creation (2 Corinthians 5:17). Ezekiel 36:26 promises a new heart and the gift of the Spirit, fulfilled in the new covenant. Jesus said, “Blessed are the poor in spirit” (Matthew 5:3), and told the story of the tax collector who cried, “God, be merciful to me, a sinner!” (Luke 18:13).
application:
Use this psalm as a pattern for confession. Pray through it slowly, line by line.

Ask for more than forgiveness. Ask for a clean heart and a right spirit.

Thank God that he does not despise a broken and contrite heart.
prayerPrompts: Pray Psalm 51 in your own words, naming what needs cleansing.
Ask him to create a clean heart and a right spirit in you.
Ask him not to take his Spirit from you, and thank him for Jesus.
